name: Omar Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. It's all confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Calder Accounts, nine of us in a unit on the industrial estate between a tyre place and a gym. Nearly all my clients are in construction: scaffolders, groundworkers, roofers, a couple of small builders. I do their accounts and tax returns, and the construction tax scheme, where the main contractor holds back some of a worker's pay for tax and I sort out the refunds. I use AI all day, for reading invoices, drafting letters, checking returns. Derek, who owns the firm, calls me the robot whisperer.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my brother Yusuf, who's a scaffolder. I'm single, I coach an under-twelves football team on Sundays, and I go to the mosque on Fridays when work allows. Money's tight because Derek pays below the going rate and I lent Yusuf most of my savings for his tickets and training, so I've got maybe two weeks' worth. There aren't many firms round here, but I've always fancied having my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful and anyone who isn't using them is leaving money on the table. At work I'd keep showing Derek what they can do. Online I don't bother much, but in the group chat with the lads I'd say it's a power tool, not a builder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a bit of a let-down, because I was counting on it to help me start my own firm. Without the big changes, I'm still on lower pay at Calder with two weeks saved. The robots aren't the problem, the payslip is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start doing books for a few of Yusuf's scaffolding mates in the evenings, using my own AI setup, at a fair price. I'd ask Derek for a proper raise, with numbers showing how much time I save the firm. And I'd get Yusuf to start paying me back, fifty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about the future, about this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Derek take a request for a raise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Derek's old school and tight, but he's fair if you show him figures. I'd show him I clear forty percent more returns than the others. If he says no, that's my answer about whether to go on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is asking Yusuf to pay you back awkward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. He's my little brother and he's done well, he's earning decent money now on the scaffolds. Family helps family, but family also pays back. My dad would say the same.

say: The tools are useful, and non-users are leaving **money on the table**.
He'd tell the lads AI is a **power tool**, not a builder.
think: It'd be a **let-down**, since he hoped AI would help him start a firm.
His problem is the **payslip**, not robots.
do: Do **evening books** for Yusuf's scaffolding mates with his own AI setup.
Ask Derek for a **raise** backed by figures.
Get Yusuf to repay **fifty a week**.
feel: Uneasy about **this month**, not the future.
S0.quote: The robots aren't the problem, the payslip is.
fieldNote: Omar's unease is about **low pay** and the money lent to his brother.
He'd use AI to build **side income** from his brother's trade network.
His values show in **family helps family**, but family also pays back.

steps.text: Do evening bookkeeping for Yusuf's scaffolding mates
Run his own AI setup to process those clients' invoices
Collect fifty a week from Yusuf to rebuild savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best time in years to start a business. Small firms can now do what big firms do. I'd tell the lads at football and the young ones I coach to learn a trade or learn the tools, ideally both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is my chance. Calder would shrink, because Derek would need fewer of us, but I'd rather be the one running a tiny firm with good software than one of the ones Derek, my boss, keeps. The risk is I've got no money behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first six months building up twenty or thirty construction clients on the side, all on AI. Once that covers my rent, I'd leave Calder and go on my own. I'd put whatever I earn back into the business, a better laptop and the paid software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit nervous about the money, but excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if it doesn't cover your rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I stay at Calder longer and keep building. I'm not stupid, I wouldn't quit on two weeks' savings. I'd want three months in the bank before I hand in my notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take clients from Calder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Derek gave me my first proper job and I won't steal his clients. I'd find my own, through Yusuf and the football parents. That's how business should work.

say: This is the best time in years to **start a business**.
He'd tell the young players he coaches to learn a trade or **the tools**.
think: This is **his chance**: run a small firm rather than be one Derek keeps.
The risk is having **no money** behind him.
do: Build **twenty or thirty** construction clients on the side in six months.
Leave Calder once side income **covers rent** and three months are saved.
Reinvest earnings in a **better laptop** and paid software.
feel: Mostly **excited**, a bit nervous about money.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the one running a tiny firm with good software than one of the ones Derek, my boss, keeps.
fieldNote: Omar sees Steady Disruption as an **opportunity**, so uneasy, not anxious.
He won't quit without **three months saved**, a sensible line for him.
He refuses to **poach clients**, showing his idea of fair business.

steps.text: Sign up twenty construction clients on the side within six months
Leave Calder Accounts once three months' rent is saved
Buy a better laptop and paid accounting software for his firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market's moving faster than anyone can keep up, and people need to get practical fast. I don't want handouts, but I'd want the government to make it easy to start a business or an apprenticeship. I'd tell everyone to learn a trade, quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years kills my plan. If AI does everything an accountant does, nobody needs a small firm like mine, they just need the software. My whole job is thinking work, so I'd be out in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd earn whatever I can in the next year setting firms up on AI, because that's a short-lived job but a real one. Then I'd go into business with Yusuf, a small scaffolding firm, me on the money side and on the scaffolds when needed. That buys us until 2031, when robots come for hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I had a plan and it's gone, and I've got two weeks' money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you actually climb scaffolding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, yes. I did it summers with Yusuf when I was at uni. It's hard on the body, but it's honest work, and in that picture it's the only thing that lasts a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the kids you coach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the kids I coach to learn a trade, stay fit and look after their families, because the computer can't do any of that yet.

say: People must get **practical fast** as the market outruns everyone.
Government should make it easy to start a **business or apprenticeship**, not give handouts.
think: Two years **kills his plan**, since nobody needs a small firm.
His work is all thinking work, so he's **out in 2028**.
do: Earn in year one setting firms up on **AI**.
Start a **scaffolding firm** with Yusuf, doing money and site work.
Use the **three-year gap** before robots for hands-on income.
feel: Alarmed, with **no plan** left and only two weeks' money.
S2.quote: I'd tell the kids I coach to learn a trade, stay fit and look after their families, because the computer can't do any of that yet.
fieldNote: Omar's adaptability doesn't help when AGI removes the **whole job**, so he's alarmed.
He moves quickly to a **hands-on** bridge with his brother.
He wants government to **enable**, not support: start-ups and apprenticeships.

steps.text: Set up small firms on AI accounting tools for one year
Start a scaffolding firm with Yusuf, handling money and site work
Leave Calder Accounts once the scaffolding firm is running

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but it's enough for anyone with get-up-and-go. Start a business, learn a trade, build something your family can rely on. I'd say it to the football parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is three good years for me, then a hard turn. I'd start my own firm now, earn well for two or three years, and then shift into something hands-on before 2031. The trick is to use the good years to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch my own little practice in year one, AI doing the grunt work, aiming for forty construction clients. I'd save a third of everything. And by year three I'd put some of it into a scaffolding business with Yusuf, so we've got something ready when the accounting dries up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in the good way. I like a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't it risky to start a business you know will end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every business ends sometime, so you make money while it's there and move on. My dad ran a market stall for twenty years and then the market closed. Five years is enough to make a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Derek say when you leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Derek would grumble and then wish me luck. He might even send me the clients he can't be bothered with. Derek's sixty-one, so in this picture he'd probably sell up anyway.

say: Five years is enough for anyone with **get-up-and-go**.
He'd tell the football parents to build something their **family** can rely on.
think: He'd get **three good years**, then need a hard turn.
The trick is using the good years to **save**.
do: Launch his own **AI-run practice** in year one, aiming for forty clients.
Save **a third** of everything he earns.
Invest in a **scaffolding business** with Yusuf by year three.
feel: Anxious in a **good way**; he likes a deadline.
S3.quote: Every business ends sometime, so you make money while it's there and move on.
fieldNote: Omar plans a **dated pivot** from his own practice to scaffolding by 2031.
His dad's **market stall** shapes his view that businesses end.
His income could still realistically shrink, so **anxious**, though he feels in control.

steps.text: Leave Calder and launch his own construction accounting practice
Save a third of all practice income
Put savings into a scaffolding business with Yusuf by year three
Run the practice's routine bookkeeping entirely on AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for people who like to work. Plenty of time to build a business, learn a trade, raise a family. I'd tell young lads not to waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's the best picture. I'd have six or seven good years running my own firm, maybe hiring two people. Then I'd sell the client list before 2036 and move into something with my hands or my own business with Yusuf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Calder for a year while I build up clients on the side. Then I'd go on my own and invest in good software. And I'd save properly for once, ten percent minimum, because I'd want a deposit on a house before I'm thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, if anything. It's a good picture for me, but the money's still thin today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire people knowing their jobs go by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them straight. Work here for five years, learn the business, and I'll help you find the next thing. That's better than most firms would offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the house mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A house means I can marry, have kids, have my parents round for dinner. My dad always said a man should own the roof over his head, and I agree with him. It's old-fashioned, I know.

say: Ten years is a **gift** for people who like to work.
He'd tell young lads not to **waste** a decade meant for building businesses and families.
think: He'd have six or seven **good years** running his own firm.
He'd **sell the client list** before 2036 and move on.

Go on his own and **invest in software**.

S4.quote: My dad always said a man should own the roof over his head, and I agree with him.
fieldNote: Omar expects to **do well** in this picture, so only thin savings keep him uneasy.
He'd be **honest with staff** about how long their jobs last.
A **house** is tied to marriage and family in his plans.

steps.text: Build side clients for a year while still at Calder
Invest in paid AI accounting software for his own firm
Save ten percent of income for a house deposit
Sell his practice's client list before 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it kills my business before it starts. What would help is cheap, quick ways to start a business and paid apprenticeships for adults, not benefits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the lads on site. My clients are scaffolders and roofers who hate paperwork. Scaffolders and roofers will be the last to get replaced and the first to get ripped off by dodgy AI tax apps. Someone needs to look out for them.

headlineQuote: Scaffolders and roofers will be the last to get replaced and the first to get ripped off by dodgy AI tax apps.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old** accountant at a nine-person firm serving **construction workers**.
He shares a flat with his brother Yusuf, a scaffolder, after lending him most of his **savings**.
He uses AI all day and dreams of **his own firm**.
He believes in **work, family and enterprise**, and wants help starting businesses, not benefits.
He sees most scenarios as **opportunity**, except AGI by 2028, which leaves him alarmed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which kills his **business** before it starts.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap business start-up** routes and paid adult apprenticeships.
